To scuff means to lightly scrape or rub a surface in a way that damages or marks it. The key idea is surface-level damage — not a deep scratch, not a break, but a dull, rough, or discolored patch left behind from friction.

Think of it this way: when two things rub against each other carelessly, the softer or less protected one gets scuffed.

1. To damage a surface by scraping or rubbing against it

This is the most common use. When you scuff something, you've accidentally — or carelessly — scraped its surface, leaving a visible mark or blemish.

  • He scuffed his brand-new leather shoes on the edge of the step.
  • The workers scuffed the hardwood floor while moving the sofa.
  • Be careful not to scuff the wall when you carry that box through the door.

The damage here is specific: it's not a deep gash or a crack. It's more like the surface has been lightly roughed up — the shine is gone from that spot, the colour looks dull, or there's a faint scratch. This is why you often hear about shoes and floors getting scuffed — they have smooth, polished surfaces that show this kind of damage very easily.

2. To drag or shuffle your feet while walking

The second meaning describes how someone walks — specifically, walking without properly lifting your feet, so your soles drag and scrape along the ground as you move.

  • The tired child scuffed along the hallway toward bed.
  • She scuffed her feet across the kitchen floor in her old slippers.
  • He scuffed down the corridor, too exhausted to walk properly.

Notice how in this meaning, the action is about movement — it paints a picture of someone walking lazily, sluggishly, or wearily, with their feet barely leaving the ground.

They are really two sides of the same physical action. When you drag your feet (meaning 2), the bottom of your shoes keeps rubbing against the ground — and that rubbing is exactly what damages the shoes and the floor (meaning 1). So the two meanings grow naturally from one idea: repeated light scraping contact.
What Makes Scuffing Different From Similar Words

• Scratch — A scratch is usually a thin, sharp, deeper line cut into a surface, often by something with a point (a nail, a key). A scuff is broader, duller, and more of a smear or rough patch than a clean line.
  • Scrape — Scraping often involves more force and a larger area, like dragging your knee across rough concrete and tearing skin off. Scuffing is gentler and more superficial — it affects the finish or coating of a surface, not the material underneath.
  • Scratch vs. Scuff on shoes: If you drag your foot sideways on a rough step, the shoe gets scuffed — a dull, rubbed-off patch appears. If a sharp pebble cuts a narrow line into the leather, that's a scratch.

The feeling of scuffing is almost always accidental and careless — you weren't trying to damage something, it just happened because you weren't paying attention.

• Shoes — especially leather shoes, which lose their shine in that spot
  • Floors — hardwood, tiles, or laminate pick up dull grey or white drag marks
  • Walls — when furniture brushes against them or bags knock into them
  • Car bumpers and paint — from light contact in a parking lot
  • Furniture — table legs, chair corners

Imagine a child dragging their feet down a hallway. Their shoes aren't lifting — just sliding along the floor. After a few days of this:

  • The soles and toes of the shoes look rough and dull — the shoes are scuffed.
  • The floor has faint grey drag marks — the floor has been scuffed.
  • The act of walking that way — the child is scuffing along.

That's the whole word.
